Fit the depth profile derived from a steady-state carbon balance (Pillar 2b)

Source: R/piml_mechanistic.R
piml_profile_fit_mechanistic.Rd

Fits $$v \frac{dC}{dz} = I(z) - kC, \qquad I(z) = I_0 e^{-z/z_r},$$ the advection-reaction limit of the standard soil-carbon depth balance with bioturbation neglected, plus a mineral-associated floor. Equivalently $$\frac{dC}{dz} = -\lambda\,\bigl(C - [A + B e^{-z/z_r}]\bigr), \qquad \lambda = k/v,\; B = I_0/k,$$ a relaxation with a constant rate toward a depth-varying target.

Usage

piml_profile_fit_mechanistic(
  depths,
  values,
  y_surface = NULL,
  top = NULL,
  bottom = NULL,
  family = c("lognormal", "gaussian", "gamma"),
  reg = 0.001,
  control = list(maxit = 4000)
)

Arguments

depths

Numeric vector of horizon mid-depths (cm).

values

Numeric vector of concentrations, same length, strictly positive.

y_surface

Optional fixed surface value; if supplied it is not estimated.

top, bottom

Optional horizon boundaries. When supplied each datum is compared to the model's depth-average over its horizon (analytic here, since every term is an exponential) rather than to a point evaluation.

family

Observation family, as in piml_profile_fit(). Defaults to "lognormal": soil carbon is positive and right-skewed, and a Gaussian on g/kg weights every horizon by the same absolute error, so a profile spanning 30 to 2 g/kg is fitted almost entirely by its topsoil.

reg

L2 shrinkage toward the data-driven start, on the log scale.

control

stats::optim control list.

Value

An edaphos_piml_mech object with params (A, B, lambda, z_r, y0), rmse, fitted, converged, and the inputs.

Details

This is the mechanistic counterpart to piml_profile_fit(). The two differ in where the depth-dependence sits: piml_profile_fit() attenuates the rate with depth, which no process produces and which pushes its equilibrium coordinate outside the admissible range; this model attenuates the target, following root input, and every parameter is positive with a literature prior.

On accuracy the two are a tie, and the honest statement of that took two attempts. Under a Gaussian likelihood this model appeared to win decisively on leave-the-deepest-horizon-out prediction across the 875 monotone profiles in inst/extdata/piml_wosis_cerrado.rds (p = 2e-6). Correcting the likelihood for BOTH models removed the difference: RMSE 1.483 against 1.507, winning on 454 of 875 profiles against 421, paired Wilcoxon p = 0.25. The Gaussian had been penalising the attenuating-rate form more heavily, because weighting every horizon by the same absolute error hurts the model whose flexibility lies in the deep tail.

Prefer this model because it can be defended, not because it predicts better. On the nine-horizon pedon shipped with the package it does fit markedly better (RMSE 0.44 against 2.52 g/kg), but one pedon is one pedon.

What this model does not identify

lambda is the ratio \(k/v\) of the decomposition rate constant to the advection velocity, and B is the ratio \(I_0/k\) of the surface root input to the same rate constant. A depth profile alone cannot separate them: doubling both \(k\) and \(v\) leaves every prediction unchanged. The fitted numbers are therefore ratios with soil-physical meaning, not decomposition rates, and reporting lambda as a turnover rate would be wrong. Separating \(k\) from \(v\) needs an independent constraint — radiocarbon ages, a chronosequence, or a measured erosion or deposition rate — none of which is in this package.

The same applies to the neglected bioturbation term: setting \(D = 0\) is an assumption about the depth range, valid below the mixed surface layer, and it is not testable from a single profile.

References

Elzein A, Balesdent J (1995). Mechanistic simulation of vertical distribution of carbon concentrations and residence times in soils. Soil Science Society of America Journal 59:1328–1335.

Jackson RB, Canadell J, Ehleringer JR, Mooney HA, Sala OE, Schulze ED (1996). A global analysis of root distributions for terrestrial biomes. Oecologia 108:389–411.

Braakhekke MC, Beer C, Hoosbeek MR, et al. (2011). SOMPROF: a vertically explicit soil organic matter model. Ecological Modelling 222:1712–1730.

See also

piml_profile_fit() for the attenuating-rate form, and vignette("pilar2-piml-profile") for the comparison.

Examples

# A simulated Cerrado-shaped profile. This package ships no real soil
# data; see [edaphos_example_profiles()] for what these values are.
H <- edaphos_example_profiles(what = "horizons")
h <- H[H$profile_id == H$profile_id[1], ]
fit <- piml_profile_fit_mechanistic(h$depth_mid, h$soc_g_kg,
                                    top = h$top, bottom = h$bottom)
fit
#> <edaphos_piml_mech>
#>   v dC/dz = I0 exp(-z/z_r) - k C     (steady-state advection-reaction)
#>   dC/dz   = -lambda (C - [A + B exp(-z/z_r)]),  lambda = k/v, B = I0/k
#>   y0    = 45.98      A (deep floor) = 0.2467   
#>   B     = 31.49      z_r = 43.25     cm   lambda = 0.1734 /cm
#>   implied Jackson beta = 0.9771
#>   n obs = 5 (layer)       rmse = 0.4507   converged = TRUE
